books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142

stimulus.text:
“That all political disabilities imposed by the third section of the fourteenth article of amendments of the Constitution of the United States are hereby removed from all persons whomsoever, except Senators and Representatives of the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh Congresses, officers in the judicial, military, and naval service of the United States, heads of departments, and foreign ministers of the United States.”

—Amnesty Act, May 22, 1872 (17 Stat. 142)
stimulus.source_note: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142. Public domain (federal statute; text verified against the Statutes at Large as quoted by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and Congress.gov).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Congress passed the Amnesty Act with the two-thirds vote the Fourteenth Amendment required. Its passage in 1872 best shows that

options.text: Congress had given up on protecting Black voting rights entirely.
options.misconception: Congress still passed the Enforcement Acts and, in 1875, the Civil Rights Act; the turn was gradual, not total.

options.text: Northern leaders were shifting from punishment toward reconciliation with the South.
Southern Democrats had already won control of Congress.
options.misconception: Background: Republicans still held both houses in 1872; the Democrats took the House in 1874.

options.text: the Supreme Court had ordered Congress to restore Confederate officeholders.
options.misconception: Background: the Court issued no such order; Congress acted on its own.

rationales.A: Congress still passed the Enforcement Acts and, in 1875, the Civil Rights Act; the turn was gradual, not total.
rationales.B: A two-thirds vote means even many Republicans agreed to lift the penalties. Seven years after the war, the North’s mood was shifting from remaking the South to letting it govern itself again.
rationales.C: Background: Republicans still held both houses in 1872; the Democrats took the House in 1874.
rationales.D: Background: the Court issued no such order; Congress acted on its own.
rationales.general:
1. The Fourteenth Amendment demanded two-thirds of each house to lift the officeholding ban.
2. The Act passed, so that supermajority existed, including many Republicans.
3. Background: in 1872 the Liberal Republicans were already breaking with Reconstruction over corruption and fatigue.
4. The vote is the mood made visible: punishment was giving way to reconciliation.
Remember: a supermajority vote is a weather vane, and this one pointed toward letting the South go.
